title: Identify pest/s encountered and assess the infestation impact

lessons.title: Identifying pests in the field
lessons.html:
From evidence to identification

In practice the officer often finds signs before the pest itself. Identification should move from evidence to confirmation: interpret the signs, find or trap specimens, and confirm the species or group to the level needed for a control decision.

Step 1: interpret the evidence

EvidencePoints to
Droppings by size and shapeNorway rat, roof rat or mouse; cockroach specks; bird droppings
Exit holes in kernelsInternal grain feeders such as weevils and lesser grain borer
Webbing and frass in stored productStored product moths
Mud tubes, soil-packed galleriesSubterranean termites
Round holes and powdery frass in timberWood boring beetles
Hexagonal pelletsDrywood termites
Blood spots on mattress seamsBed bugs

Step 2: find or capture specimens

  • Search harbourages with a torch at the right time; cockroaches and rodents are mostly active at night.
  • Sieve grain samples onto a white tray and examine with a hand lens.
  • Place sticky monitors or pheromone traps and return to read them.
  • Collect specimens in labelled vials with date, site and exact location.

Step 3: confirm identification

Use key features: body shape, size, colour, antennae, snout, wing covers and markings. Compare with reference guides and pictorial keys. For example, distinguish the German cockroach (small, light brown, two dark stripes behind the head) from the American cockroach (large, reddish-brown). Distinguish primary grain pests, which attack whole kernels, from secondary pests that feed on broken grain and dust.

When identification is uncertain, or when it carries regulatory consequences, such as a suspected quarantine pest in export grain or a suspected European house borer in the Western Cape, submit specimens to a specialist or laboratory and handle the situation as your procedures require.

Avoid common errors

  • Do not assume the species from previous visits; pest populations change.
  • Do not mistake beneficial insects or harmless species for pests.
  • Do not conclude current activity from old damage alone.

lessons.title: Assessing the extent of the infestation
lessons.html:
How big is the problem?

Once the pest is identified, the officer must estimate how widespread and severe the infestation is. This determines whether action is needed, how urgent it is and what scale of intervention is required.

Measuring extent

  • Distribution: mark every finding on the site plan. Is the problem confined to one room, one bin or one stack, or is it spread through the site?
  • Density: count insects per kilogram of grain sample, rodents caught or baits taken per station, cockroaches per sticky trap, or termite activity points.
  • Life stages: the presence of eggs, larvae, nymphs and adults indicates an established, breeding population.
  • Trend: compare with previous monitoring data. Is the population rising, stable or falling?

Activity rating

Use a consistent scale, such as none, low, moderate and high, defined in your company procedure, so that ratings are comparable between visits and officers.

Identifying the cause

Record why the pest is present: spillage and poor sanitation, damp grain, broken proofing, poor stock rotation, clutter, leaks, soil contact with timber or uncontrolled refuse. Treatment without addressing the cause usually fails.

Worked example

At a maize silo complex, sieved samples from bin 6 show eight live maize weevils per kilogram at the top layer and two per kilogram at mid-depth, with larvae found inside dissected kernels. Bins 5 and 7 show none. The grain temperature cable in bin 6 shows a warm zone near the top. Previous monthly samples showed no insects. This describes a localised but established and rising infestation in one bin, likely linked to a moisture pocket and residual grain left in the bin before filling. The extent statement would record the bin, depths, density, life stages, trend and probable cause, which together guide whether to fumigate bin 6 and how urgently.

lessons.title: Assessing impact and reporting
lessons.html:
What is the impact?

Impact assessment considers the consequences of the infestation for the client, people and the environment.

Impact typeExamples
HealthRodent-borne disease, cockroach allergens, contaminated food
Product loss and qualityGrain mass loss, heating, mould, downgrading, insect fragments
Commercial and regulatoryFailed audits, rejected consignments, closure by environmental health, loss of export certification
StructuralWeakened roof timbers, damaged cables, blocked gutters
ReputationalCustomer complaints, social media exposure

Assessing risk level

Combine the likelihood of harm with its severity. A few secondary beetles in a feed store may be low risk; a single rat in a food production area, or live primary pests in grain about to be loaded for export, is high risk and urgent. Consider the sensitivity of the site and of people present.

Reporting the assessment

  1. State the pest identified and how identification was confirmed.
  2. Describe the extent: locations, density, life stages and trend.
  3. State the cause or conducive conditions.
  4. Describe the impact and risk level.
  5. Recommend actions with priorities: immediate, short-term and long-term, separating client actions from pest management interventions.

Discuss urgent findings with the responsible manager before leaving the site, then provide the written report promptly. Keep specimens or photographs as evidence where appropriate.

Key points

  • Move from evidence to specimens to confirmed identification.
  • Use key features and reference guides; send uncertain or regulatory specimens to a specialist.
  • Measure distribution, density, life stages and trend, and identify the cause.
  • Assess health, product, commercial, structural and reputational impacts.
  • Report risk level and prioritised recommendations, and escalate urgent risks immediately.

quiz.question: Which features identify the German cockroach?

options.text: Small, light brown, with two dark stripes behind the head

quiz.question: Hexagonal pellets below timber point to...
What does finding eggs, larvae and adults together indicate?

options.text: A population that is dying out
A few secondary beetles in a feed store
Old exit holes in a garden fence
Live primary pests in grain about to be loaded for export
One fly in a warehouse office

quiz.question: Why should the cause of an infestation be recorded?

options.text: Treatment usually fails if the cause is not addressed

quiz.question: You should assume the same pest is present as on the previous visit without checking.
A single rat in a food production area should be treated as an urgent, high-risk finding.
